pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 5–7; Storm Safety (CONCEPTUAL/safety, 0.007): basic thunderstorm safety — during thunder and lightning go indoors or into a car, stay away from trees and water; storms can be frightening but there are ways to stay safe.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS1 weather observation + PSHE 'keeping safe'; storm safety is PSHE/personal-safety content rather than a KS1 science statutory bullet. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS): relates to K-ESS3-2 (prepare for and respond to severe weather; NOT fetched this session, verified:false). The science of thunder/lightning is the 7-9 topic; here the payload is the SAFETY RULES and emotional reassurance.
• Operational details — Two payloads: (1) a small set of clear, correct safety rules — get inside a building or car; stay away from tall trees, open ground, and water (pools, ponds, the sea); (2) reassurance — storms are loud and can be scary but are natural, and following simple rules keeps you safe. Teach WHY going indoors is safest in child terms (lightning is more likely to hit tall/open/wet things; a building or car protects you). Avoid myths (a tree is NOT shelter; don't stand under it). Keep it calm and empowering, not fear-inducing. Prerequisite: Types of Weather (storms); feeds Thunder & Lightning (7-9, the science). Evidence: state ≥2 thunderstorm safety rules; explain why indoors is safest; describe storms as natural events you can be safe in.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (concrete/procedural + emotional): the child states at least two thunderstorm safety rules, explains that going indoors (or into a car) is safest, and frames storms as natural events they can stay safe during — knowing the right action and feeling reassured rather than frightened.
bestPractices: Teach a SHORT, memorable rule set (inside a building or car; away from trees, open ground and water) — few rules, clearly correct, rehearsed.
Pair each rule with a child-level WHY (lightning tends to hit tall, open or wet things, so we go inside where it's protected) so rules are understood, not just recited.
Bust the dangerous 'shelter under a tree' myth explicitly — a tree is one of the LEAST safe places in a storm.

Handle FEAR directly and calmly: name that thunder is loud and can feel scary, explain thunder is just the sound (it can't hurt you), and emphasise that knowing what to do helps you feel safe and in control.
Rehearse the safe response as a simple decision ('storm coming → go inside') through role-play/scenario, since rehearsal makes recall likelier when it matters.
Keep the physics minimal here (why lightning is dangerous) and defer the thunder-lightning science to the 7-9 topic; this topic is about action and reassurance.
keyRepresentations: A safe/unsafe place sorter: building, car (safe) vs under a tree, open field, swimming pool (unsafe).
A simple 'storm coming → go inside' action sequence/flow.
Calm reassurance scene: a child safe indoors watching a storm through the window, 'thunder is just a loud sound'.
Rule cards with matching why-icons (tall tree = lightning target; car/building = protected).
commonMisconceptions: 'Shelter under a tree to stay dry/safe' — a dangerous myth; trees are among the worst places in a thunderstorm.
'Thunder can hurt you' — thunder is only the SOUND; the danger is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
'Water is fine to be in/near during a storm' — pools, ponds and the sea are unsafe; get out and away from water.
'If you can't see rain it's safe' — lightning can strike from a storm that's still some distance away; go in when you hear thunder.
'Storms are out to get you / are a punishment' — animistic fear; storms are natural, and simple rules keep you safe.

learn.summary: Thunderstorm safety for ages 5–7: children learn a short, correct set of safety rules (go inside a building or a hard-topped car; stay away from tall trees, open ground, and water such as pools, ponds and the sea), each paired with a child-level reason (lightning tends to hit the tallest thing around, and being on open ground or in or near water leaves you exposed; a building or hard-topped car carries lightning around you into the ground), plus calm emotional reassurance that storms are natural and following simple rules helps keep you safe. The core activity is rehearsing the decision 'hear thunder → go inside', complemented by a safe/unsafe place sort to confirm the rules. This is PSHE/personal-safety content; the thunder/lightning science is a later topic.

activities.title: Storm scenario: choose where to go
feedback: Safe choice: 'You're inside and safe — now you can watch the storm from indoors, a little way back from the window.'
Tree choice: 'A tall tree is one of the riskiest places in a storm because lightning tends to hit the tallest thing — let's get inside instead.'
Water/open-ground choice: 'Open ground and water aren't safe in a storm — head for a building or a car.'
Keep every corrective message calm and empowering, never frightening.
activities.rationale: Safety is a set of decisions, so letting a child make and rehearse the choice with immediate, kind feedback lets them actively enact the response rather than only hear a list; this is intended to build recall and a sense of control. Rehearsing the response as a simple decision is intended to make it more likely to be recalled when it matters. (Efficacy here is a research-informed proposal, not a validated result.)
sourceClaims: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.
learnerActions: Watch or imagine a storm rolling in — dark clouds gather and a rumble of thunder sounds.
Choose where to go: a house, a car, under a big tree, an open field, or beside a swimming pool.
When you choose a safe place (house or car), see yourself safe and cosy indoors, watching the storm from a little way back from the window.
When you choose an unsafe place, read the kind, un-scary prompt explaining why it is risky (e.g. 'a tall tree is one of the riskiest places — let's get inside instead') and try again.
Repeat the 'hear thunder → go inside' decision several times until it feels familiar.
activities.intendedInsight: Staying safe in a storm is a decision you can make and rehearse: go indoors or into a car, and the right action becomes familiar so you feel in control rather than frightened.

activities.title: Safe place / unsafe place sort
feedback: Correct sort: confirm the rule and its reason, e.g. 'Right — a building protects you because if lightning hits it, the building carries the lightning around you and down into the ground.'
Tree placed as safe: 'A tree shelters you from rain but NOT from lightning — it's actually one of the least safe places.'
activities.rationale: Categorising places checks the rule set and surfaces the dangerous 'shelter under a tree' myth, distinguishing rain-shelter logic from lightning safety. A sort can check and reinforce this classification; the 'say the reason aloud' step is added because the sort alone does not elicit the child's own explanation.
sourceClaims: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.
learnerActions: Sort places and things into 'safe in a storm' and 'not safe in a storm'.
Safe: inside a building, inside a hard-topped car.
Unsafe: under a tall tree, in an open field, in or beside a swimming pool, pond or the sea.
For each one, say the reason aloud — e.g. 'a tall tree is unsafe because lightning tends to hit tall things'.
activities.intendedInsight: A tree is for rain shelter, not storm safety; the safe places are indoors or a car, and open or wet places are dangerous.

activities.title: Calm reassurance: thunder is just a sound
feedback: 'Thunder is just a loud noise — it can't hurt you, but it tells you lightning is near. The danger is lightning, and being inside keeps you safe.'
'Storms are natural. There are safe places to go — buildings and hard-topped cars — so you can act and stay safe.'
If a conversational persona is used, keep it strictly bounded to correct, calm storm-safety guidance.
activities.rationale: Handling fear directly and calmly — naming that thunder is loud, explaining it is only a sound, and emphasising agency — addresses the emotional reassurance goal alongside the safety rules. A caring persona may help the fear dimension but needs careful guard-railing for an anxious young child.
learnerActions: Look at a scene of a child safe indoors, watching a storm from inside.
Hear or read the message that thunder is just a loud sound — it can't hurt you, but hearing it means lightning is near; the thing to stay away from is lightning, and being indoors protects you.
Talk about how storms are natural events, not something out to get you, and that knowing what to do helps you feel safe.
Optionally ask a caring, reassuring character a worry such as 'is thunder going to hurt me?' and talk through what to do.
activities.intendedInsight: Storms can feel scary because they are loud, but thunder is only the sound; following simple rules helps keep you safe, so you can feel in control.

activities.title: What should you do? quick check
feedback: Correct: confirm and extend — 'Yes, go indoors or to a car, and stay away from tall trees and water.'

Partial (knows to go in but not why): add the reason — 'Lightning tends to hit tall things out in the open, and a building or hard-topped car carries the lightning around you into the ground, so inside you're protected.'
activities.rationale: A targeted question confirms the two-rules evidence target and the reasoning behind going indoors; used here during teaching as a check, not only as end assessment. Recognising the right choice checks knowledge of the rule but does not by itself guarantee the child can act on it, which is why the scenario rehearsal is the core activity.
sourceClaims: Thunderstorm safety: go indoors (a substantial building) or into a hard-topped car; avoid tall isolated trees, open areas, and water; 'when thunder roars, go indoors'; wait before going back out.
learnerActions: Answer: 'What should you do when you hear thunder?' — choosing 'go inside a building or car' over unsafe options.
Explain in your own words why indoors is safer than being out in the open.
Name one more thing to stay away from (tall trees, open ground, or water).
activities.intendedInsight: You can state at least two thunderstorm safety rules and say why indoors is safest.

constraints: Keep the rule set short, clearly correct and rehearsed; pair every rule with a child-level reason so rules are understood, not just recited.
Keep the tone calm, empowering and never fear-inducing; corrective feedback must reassure, not frighten.
Keep physics minimal here (only why lightning is dangerous); defer the thunder/lightning science to the later 7–9 topic.
This is a safety-rehearsal scaffold, not a substitute for a real safety conversation with a trusted adult — the digital rehearsal supports that conversation, it does not replace it.
A static reveal or reference scene can present the rules and reassurance but describes the action rather than exercising it; pair it with an activity where the child enacts the decision.
If a conversational persona is used with an anxious young child, bound it strictly to correct, calm storm-safety guidance.
Where an indoor reassurance scene is shown, keep the child a little way back from windows and doors in line with lightning-safety guidance; being inside is the key safety point.
Prerequisite: Types of Weather (storms). This feeds the later Thunder & Lightning science topic.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Source claims for NGSS K-ESS3-2 and NWS/CDC lightning guidance were marked verified:false in the original (not fetched this session); treat as legacy, not freshly confirmed.

Independent review refined the indoor reassurance image so the child watches from a little way back from the window, consistent with the lightning-safety 'stay away from windows and doors' point; the cosy indoor image was preserved rather than removed.

Safety messaging: 'wait before going back out' appears in the original safety source but was not foregrounded in the legacy activities; consider adding a 'stay inside until the storm has passed' beat for completeness. The '30 minutes after last thunder' specifics are not stated in the source and should not be invented.

One source note said lightning can strike from a storm still some distance away ('if you can't see rain it's safe' misconception); this nuance may be advanced for 5–7 but is correct and could be gently included ('go in when you hear thunder, even if it's not raining yet').
Claims that the scenario rehearsal builds recall are untested here and are stated as intended/proposed rather than asserted as established fact.

probeDeeper: Why is being indoors or in a car safer than being out in the open?
Name one more place or thing to stay away from in a thunderstorm.
Are storms something to be terrified of, or something we can stay safe in — what makes the difference?
assess.correctAnswer: No — a tall tree is one of the most dangerous places to be in lightning, because lightning tends to strike the tallest thing around. You should go indoors or into a car, and stay away from trees and water. That keeps you away from where lightning is most likely to hit.

errorPatterns.pattern: Tree as safe shelter — 'stand under a tall tree in a storm'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish rain shelter from lightning safety: lightning hits the tallest thing, so a tall tree is dangerous; head indoors or to a car instead.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — stand under the tall tree, it will shelter you.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Chooses the tree because it shelters from rain, ignoring lightning

errorPatterns.pattern: Underestimates lightning — 'a storm is just rain, you only get wet'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name lightning as electricity that can be dangerous, so a thunderstorm is more than getting wet — it's a reason to get inside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats a thunderstorm as only a rain problem, not a lightning danger

errorPatterns.pattern: Nowhere is safe / panic — 'you'll get hit no matter what'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reassure with agency: storms are natural and there ARE safe places — indoors and cars are safe; you can act to stay safe.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Sees storms as hopeless danger with no safe action

responseLevels.gap: Chooses the tree or another exposed spot; treats a storm as only rain or as hopeless danger.
responseLevels.full: Rejects the tree, chooses indoors/car, explains lightning strikes the tallest or most exposed things, adds staying away from water and tall objects, and frames storms as natural events you can be safe in.
responseLevels.partial: Knows to go indoors but can't say why, or gives one safety rule without the reason that lightning hits tall things.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A big thunderstorm with lightning starts while you're playing in the park. A child says, 'Let's stand under that big tall tree to stay safe.' Is that a good idea? What should you do instead, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands lightning safety rejects the tree and heads for indoors or a car. A child using everyday 'tree = shelter' logic picks the tree — the tell — targeting the specific documented error rather than a vague 'be careful'.
